blocks.text: The **acromioclavicular (AC) joint** joins the outer end of the collarbone (clavicle) to the acromion, the bony tip of the shoulder blade. It is supported by the AC ligaments and the stronger **coracoclavicular (CC) ligaments**. An **AC joint injury** (often called shoulder separation, not shoulder dislocation) usually follows a fall onto the point of the shoulder or a blow in contact sport [Ref - to verify]. **AC joint osteoarthritis** is a separate, gradual condition more common in older people or heavy lifters.

Doctors grade traumatic injuries by X-ray using the **Rockwood classification** (types I to VI). In general: type I is a sprain with no displacement; type II involves a torn AC ligament with mild displacement; type III involves torn AC and CC ligaments with the collarbone clearly raised; types IV to VI involve greater displacement in different directions [Ref - to verify].

items: Pain directly over the top of the shoulder at the AC joint, after a fall or hit on the shoulder.
A step or bump at the joint in higher-grade injuries.
Pain with lifting the arm across the body and above the head, and lying on that side.
In chronic or arthritic cases: aching on top of the shoulder, worse with overhead and cross-body movements, clicking, local tenderness.

rows: How did it happen? Fall onto the shoulder or arm?
Can you point to the pain with one finger?
Local AC pain is typically well localised
Is there a bump or deformity?
Any pain in the neck, numbness or arm weakness?
Any chest, breathing or swallowing difficulty after a hit to the collarbone area?
Is this a gradual ache without injury?
Heavy lifting or overhead sport history?

items: Observe for deformity, skin tenting, swelling, bruising and shoulder drooping.
Palpate the AC joint, the clavicle along its length, the sternoclavicular joint and the coracoid.
Active and passive range (often painful and limited at end range).
Cross-body adduction (below).
Cervical and neurological screen.
Rotator cuff and biceps tests to exclude associated problems.

blocks.text: E1. Palpation of the AC joint

Palpate the joint line at the end of the clavicle with the thumb. **Positive:** well-localised tenderness that reproduces the patient's pain. Tenderness is common and a positive result alone does not show the grade.
E2. Cross-body adduction test

rows: Compress the AC joint to see whether it reproduces pain
Sitting or standing; arm raised to 90 degrees forward flexion
Passively move the arm across the chest toward the opposite shoulder
Pain located on top of the shoulder at the AC joint
No pain, or pain located elsewhere such as the back of the shoulder (posterior capsule tightness)
AC joint pain when combined with local tenderness
Also painful in cuff and posterior shoulder conditions; interpret with location [Ref - to verify]

blocks.text: E3. O'Brien active compression test

rows: Help separate AC joint pain from deeper (labral or biceps anchor) pain
Standing; arm flexed to 90 degrees, adducted about 10 to 15 degrees, elbow straight
Step 1: arm internally rotated (thumb down); the therapist applies a downward force that the patient resists. Step 2: repeat with the palm up (arm externally rotated)
Pain on top of the shoulder in the thumb-down position that is reduced or gone with palm up
Pain or clicking deep in the shoulder that is reduced with palm up
Accuracy varies and the test is debated [Ref - to verify]

blocks.text: E4. Piano key sign (visual)
In higher-grade injuries, the end of the clavicle may spring back when pressed down. Do not push hard; this is a sign for doctors and imaging.
E5. Imaging
X-ray (with or without weight) and other imaging are ordered by a doctor to grade the injury and to exclude fractures.

rows: Pain along the bone, bump, bruising, unable to lift arm
Pain at the chest end of the collarbone
Medical review; urgent if airway or vascular symptoms
Anterior pain, tenderness over the groove
Weightlifters with gradual pain and tenderness

sections.title: G. RED FLAGS AND URGENT CONDITIONS

rows: Skin tenting or severely raised bone end
Do not manipulate; refer same day
Visible clavicle deformity, bruising along bone, cannot lift arm
Support the arm; refer for imaging
Hand numb, pale, cold, pulseless, or severe swelling
Chest pain, breathlessness, difficulty swallowing after trauma
Weight loss, constant night pain, cancer history

sections.title: H. Working diagnosis and decision pathway

items: Any emergency or urgent flag? **Yes:** act as in Section G.

Local AC tenderness, a fall onto the shoulder, painful cross-body test, no fracture signs? **Yes:** working diagnosis is AC joint sprain or separation. Ask a doctor for imaging when deformity is present or grading will change management.
Type I or II (minimal displacement)? **Yes:** conservative care.
Type III: shared decision between conservative care and surgery after specialist review [Ref - to verify].
Types IV to VI, skin compromise or neurovascular signs: urgent orthopaedic review.
Gradual onset and arthritis picture: manage as AC joint osteoarthritis or overuse.

rows: Soft-tissue work around the shoulder (upper trapezius, pectoral)

blocks.text: **Preferred starting choice:** protection, pain control and early graded movement and strengthening. Manual therapy has little role in acute AC injury. Do not use techniques that stress the AC joint or force a displaced bone end.

sections.title: J. Exercise prescription (example starting plan, not universal)

rows: 1: protect (type I to II: about the first days to weeks according to pain)
Pendulum, pain-free elbow and hand movement, scapular setting
Support the arm; avoid lifting and cross-body positions
Short bouts, several times a day
Isometric then banded rotation; rows; serratus punch
Overhead loading, push-ups, carries, sport drills
Meets criteria for sport or work

blocks.text: **Avoid early:** heavy cross-body movements, bench press and push-up loads, direct blows and contact sport until pain and strength allow. No fixed time to return is stated; criteria are full range, near-normal strength, no pain with sport movements, and doctor clearance for contact sport [Ref - to verify].
A sling may be used for comfort for a short period. Long use is not recommended because it can lead to stiffness [Ref - to verify].
Injections for AC osteoarthritis and surgery for higher grades are medical decisions.

items: **Visit 1:** screen flags, examine, refer for imaging if needed, protect and educate.
**Early:** pain control, short-term sling for comfort, early gentle movement.
**Middle:** restore full range and scapular control, add strength.
**Late:** return to work or sport with gradual load; contact athletes get doctor clearance.
**If not improving or high grade:** orthopaedic review.

blocks.text: Record pain, AC tenderness, cross-body pain, range, strength, scapular control and function; a shoulder outcome measure such as QuickDASH [Ref - to verify].

rows: Pain lower, range and strength improving
Persistent pain on top of the shoulder after months
Medical review, consider injection or imaging
New neurological signs or increasing deformity

blocks.text: **Case:** A 28-year-old cyclist fell onto the point of his left shoulder. Pain is localised to the AC joint and he has a small raised bump. Cross-body adduction is painful at the top of the shoulder. Passive elevation is limited by pain. No numbness, no breathing problems, normal pulses. X-ray shows mild AC separation without fracture.

**Working diagnosis:** AC joint sprain (grade II type). **Plan:** short-term sling for comfort, early pain-guided movement, scapular and cuff strengthening, avoid loading across the body early, progressive return to cycling and gym.
**Questions and answers**

items: Why is a shoulder separation not the same as a shoulder dislocation? A separation affects the joint between the collarbone and shoulder blade, while a dislocation involves the ball and socket joint.
Why check along the whole clavicle? A fracture can look like an AC injury and needs different management.
Why avoid mobilising the AC joint? It is an injured, painful stabilising joint, and forcing it may increase pain and displacement.
Skin tenting over the bone end. What now? Refer urgently the same day because the skin is at risk.
The patient wants to know if surgery is needed. For types I and II conservative care is usual; higher grades need specialist input [Ref - to verify].
**Initial approach:** protection, pain control and early graded movement.
**Justifying findings:** local tenderness, mechanism, painful cross-body test, no fracture signs.
**Priority:** restore range, scapular control and strength.
**Manual therapy:** minimal; avoid direct joint stress.
**Exercise:** gentle range, scapular and cuff strengthening, sport-specific loading.
**Modalities:** limited role.
**Tell the patient:** most low-grade injuries recover well; a bump may remain.
**Avoid:** heavy cross-body loading early, prolonged sling use, forceful joint techniques.
**Measure:** pain, range, strength, function.
**If no improvement:** medical review.
**Referral triggers:** Section G.
**Discharge:** full function and strength, return to sport criteria met.

blocks.text: **Assumptions:** no fracture, no neurovascular injury, low-grade injury.

items: **Can be tested:** outcomes of conservative care versus surgery for type III injuries; accuracy of clinical tests against imaging.
**Hypotheses:** that early movement helps recovery; that scapular strengthening reduces strain on the AC joint.
**Future questions:** best management of type III and chronic AC pain.

blocks.text: Evidence not graded until references are verified.

items: Explain AC injury versus shoulder dislocation.
Perform palpation, cross-body adduction and O'Brien tests and state their limits.
Recognise injuries that need urgent referral.
